name: Gigantopithecus
fact: The largest primate ever to live - towering over even gorillas. Known only from thousands of isolated teeth found in Chinese apothecary shops sold as dragon teeth. It went extinct around 300,000 years ago likely because its bamboo forests shrank during ice age climate swings.

name: Woolly Mammoth
fact: Last population survived on Wrangel Island until 4,000 years ago. Complete genomes recovered from permafrost.
know: Carcasses frozen in the Siberian permafrost still have hair, skin, stomach contents and even a dark liquid reported as blood. Their DNA has been read in full — the oldest, from a mammoth tooth, is over a million years old.
taxonomy: Mammalia › Proboscidea › Elephantidae › Mammuthus › Mammuthus primigenius
discovery: Identified as extinct elephant species by Cuvier (1796). Genus Mammuthus coined by Joshua Brookes (1828).
keyResearchers: Cuvier, G. (1796), Blumenbach, J.F. (1799), Shapiro et al. (2004 DNA)
citation: Shapiro, B. et al. (2004). Rise and fall of the Beringian steppe bison. Science 306:1561–1565.

name: Saber-toothed Cat (Smilodon)
fact: S. fatalis known from LA Tar Pits (2,000+ specimens). Ambush predator with 7-inch canines. Hunted megafauna like bison and camels.
know: The tar pits at La Brea have yielded more than 2,000 individual Smilodon. Many had survived crippling injuries long enough for the bone to heal — which suggests, though it does not prove, that they lived in groups.
discovery: Lund named Smilodon populator 1842 from cave fossils in Brazil.
keyResearchers: Lund, P.W. (1842), Cope, E.D. (1869), Schubert et al. (2010)
citation: Lund, P.W. (1842). Mémoire sur les ossemens fossiles. Annales des Sciences Naturelles 17:40–106.
sites: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles

name: Giant Ground Sloth
fact: Bigger than an elephant when rearing up! Related to tiny modern tree sloths. Its claws were up to 50cm long — used to pull down tree branches. It went extinct shortly after humans arrived in South America.
sites: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles
West Virginia — described by Thomas Jefferson

name: Cave Lion
fact: The biggest cat that EVER lived! Cave paintings made by humans 35,000 years ago show cave lions hunting. We painted them because we competed with them for shelter. They looked us in the eye.

name: Giant Wombat (Diprotodon)
fact: A marsupial the size of a hippo! Waddled on short legs like a tank. An experiment in giant herbivores unique to Australia. When humans arrived, it went extinct in just a few centuries.

name: Woolly Rhinoceros
fact: Like a mammoth's rhino cousin! Covered in thick fur with a huge front horn for digging through snow to find grass. Lived on the Arctic steppe alongside mammoths. Vanished before written history began.
sites: Starunia, Ukraine — pickled in salt and oil

name: Arctodus (Short-Faced Bear)
fact: The largest terrestrial mammal carnivore of North America - a bear with proportionally long legs built for speed rather than tree-climbing. Arctodus may have stolen kills from other predators like a giant hyena. Its extinction coincided with the arrival of humans in the Americas.
sites: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles

name: Megaloceros (Irish Elk)
habitat: Open grasslands and forests of Eurasia
fact: The largest deer ever, with antlers spanning up to 3.7 meters - wider than a small car. The antlers grew so fast during breeding season they placed extreme demands on the male's calcium reserves. Cave paintings from France and Spain show our ancestors were familiar with these magnificent animals.

name: Glyptodon
fact: A car-sized armadillo relative encased in a dome of over 1,000 interlocking bony plates. Its bony-ringed tail may have been swung as a weapon. Early humans are known to have used the shells of dead Glyptodons as emergency shelters from storms.

name: American Mastodon
habitat: Forests and bogs of North America
fact: A forest-dwelling cousin of the mammoth with rounded teeth adapted for browsing on leaves and twigs rather than grazing on grass. Mastodon dung preserved in ancient bogs has revealed their diet in astonishing detail. Their extinction closely tracked the spread of human hunters across the Americas.
sites: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles

name: Dire Wolf (Aenocyon dirus)
habitat: Open grasslands and forests of the Americas
fact: The most common large carnivore found in the La Brea Tar Pits - over 4,000 individuals excavated. DNA analysis in 2021 revealed dire wolves were not closely related to gray wolves but were a completely distinct American lineage that went extinct at the end of the Ice Age.
sites: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles

name: Elasmotherium (Siberian Unicorn)
fact: A shaggy rhinoceros the weight of an elephant, thought to have carried a single enormous horn on its forehead.
know: It was long believed to have died out 200,000 years ago. In 2018, radiocarbon dates showed it survived until at least 39,000 years ago — so early modern humans and Neanderthals in western Asia may well have seen one.

name: Thylacoleo (Marsupial Lion)
fact: Australia's largest meat-eating mammal, with a retractable thumb claw and cheek teeth like bolt-cutters. For its size it had the strongest bite of any mammal known, living or extinct.
know: Complete skeletons lie where the animals fell into cave shafts on the Nullarbor Plain. Claw scratches on cave walls show it was also an expert climber.

name: Megalania (Giant Monitor)
fact: The largest land lizard known — a relative of the Komodo dragon, and probably venomous like it. The first people to reach Australia lived alongside it.
debate: Only scattered bones are known, so its size is scaled up from smaller relatives: published lengths run from 3.5 to 7 metres.

name: Homotherium
fact: A scimitar-toothed cat built for running. A frozen cub from Yakutia, described in 2024, still has its dark fur, big paws and small ears.

name: American Lion
fact: A lion bigger than today's, found across North America. Over 80 have been dug from the La Brea Tar Pits.
sites: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles

name: Cave Bear
fact: A huge bear that hibernated in caves — and despite its size, mostly ate plants. Some caves hold the bones of thousands.

name: Cave Hyena
fact: A large hyena that dragged prey into caves across Europe.
know: In 1821 William Buckland showed Kirkdale Cave was an ancient hyena den by comparing gnawed bones and droppings with those of a living hyena in a travelling menagerie.

name: Columbian Mammoth
fact: A giant of warmer North America, larger than the woolly mammoth and with less hair. A sinkhole in South Dakota trapped over 60 of them.
sites: Mammoth Site, Hot Springs, South Dakota

name: Straight-tusked Elephant
fact: A huge elephant of warm interglacial Europe. Its Indian cousin may have been the largest land mammal ever.

name: Doedicurus
fact: A glyptodont the size of a small car, with a spiked club on its tail.

name: Toxodon
fact: A rhino-sized grazer. Darwin bought a skull from a farmer in Uruguay for 18 pence. Proteins extracted in 2015 showed it was related to horses and rhinos.

name: Giant Beaver
fact: A beaver the size of a black bear. Its chemistry shows it ate water plants rather than cutting down trees.

name: Bison latifrons
fact: A giant bison with horns 2 m from tip to tip.

name: Camelops
fact: A North American camel. Camels evolved in North America and lived there until the end of the last ice age.
sites: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles

name: Genyornis
fact: A giant flightless bird related to ducks and geese, not emus.
debate: Burnt eggshells 50,000 years old may show early Australians cooked its eggs. Some researchers think the shells came from a different, smaller bird.

name: Procoptodon
fact: A giant short-faced kangaroo that probably walked rather than hopped, and pulled branches down with long-clawed arms.

name: Sicilian Dwarf Elephant
fact: An elephant no taller than a large dog, from Sicily and Malta. Islands with little food shrank its ancestors from 4 m to 1 m.
know: An elephant skull has one huge hole in the middle of the face, for the trunk. In 1914 the palaeontologist Othenio Abel suggested that ancient Greeks finding such skulls imagined one-eyed giants — the Cyclops.

name: Cyprus Dwarf Hippo
fact: A hippo the size of a pig that lived on Cyprus and climbed rocky hillsides.
debate: Burnt hippo bones in a rock shelter beside the earliest human tools on Cyprus suggest people finished them off. Some argue the bones gathered there naturally.

name: Myotragus (“mouse goat”)
fact: A goat relative from Mallorca and Menorca, isolated for over 5 million years. It had forward-facing eyes, a small brain and rodent-like front teeth.
know: Its bones grow in stops and starts with rest lines, like a reptile's. With no predators and little food, it may have slowed its body down to save energy (2009 study).

name: Meiolania
fact: A giant land turtle with cow-like horns on its head and a spiked club on its tail. It could not pull its head into its shell.
debate: Bones on Vanuatu, apparently eaten by people about 3,000 years ago, may be the last meiolaniids — or a different kind of turtle.

name: Palorchestes
fact: A marsupial with huge claws on its front feet and a long tongue, probably for stripping leaves and bark. It was once drawn as a giant kangaroo, then as a marsupial tapir with a trunk.
debate: A 2020 study of its skull found no sign of a trunk after all. What it really looked like is still open.

name: Giant Echidna (Murrayglossus)
fact: An egg-laying mammal the size of a sheep — the largest monotreme ever, with longer legs than today's echidnas.

name: Arctotherium
size: Up to about 3.4 m standing, 1.6 tonnes
fact: Possibly the largest bear that ever lived. Its ancestors crossed into South America over the new land bridge.

name: Shasta Ground Sloth
fact: A ground sloth of the American deserts. Mummified bodies with skin and hair survive in dry caves.
know: Rampart Cave held a deposit of its dung over a metre deep, recording thousands of years of its diet. In 1976 a visitor's fire set it alight; it smouldered for months.
sites: Aden Crater, New Mexico — a mummy

name: Teratornis
fact: A giant condor-like bird that probably hunted small animals on the ground rather than scavenging. Over 100 have been pulled from the La Brea Tar Pits.
sites: La Brea Tar Pits, Los Angeles

name: Giant Gelada (Theropithecus oswaldi)
fact: A grass-eating monkey as big as a large dog. At Olorgesailie in Kenya, stone tools lie among the bones of dozens of them — early humans ate them.

name: Palaeoloxodon namadicus
size: Perhaps 5 m tall at the shoulder
fact: A straight-tusked elephant of India’s Narmada valley that may have been the largest land mammal ever — larger even than Paraceratherium.
debate: The record size is worked out from a few incomplete bones, so it is a careful estimate, not a measurement.

name: Pygmy Giant Panda (Ailuropoda microta)
fact: The earliest known giant panda, half the size of today’s. Its teeth show it was already a bamboo specialist two million years ago.

name: Pelorovis
fact: A giant relative of the African buffalo, with curving horns each about a metre long. Early humans at Olduvai butchered them.

name: Giant Hyena (Pachycrocuta)
fact: The largest hyena that ever lived, built to drag off carcasses and crack the biggest bones. At Zhoukoudian it shared — and fought over — the caves with Peking Man.
